title: HTML: Building the Foundation
subtitle: Let's Give Our Game Its Structure

scenes.name: Lesson opener
scenes.visual: Branded lesson card: 'LESSON 2 · HTML' red tile, title 'Building the Foundation'. Flat cards slide away.

scenes.name: Welcome to Paisley Studio
scenes.visual: The full Paisley IDE with an empty project. One ring at a time: sidebar, then each of the three sidebar buttons (with a tooltip label), then a file row showing the pencil and bin, the editor, the preview, then Save and Run. The rest of the UI stays visible but is never all highlighted at once.
scenes.camera: Gentle zoom toward each highlighted area, back out between groups.
scenes.onScreen: Labels: PROJECT FILES · NEW FILE · NEW FOLDER · UPLOAD · RENAME · DELETE · CODE EDITOR · PREVIEW · SAVE · RUN

lines.text: Welcome back, future creators!
Before we start building our game, let's get comfortable with our workspace. This is Paisley Studio.
On the left, we have our project area. This is where we see and organise our files.
These three buttons at the top are very useful.
The first button creates a new file.
The second button creates a new folder. Folders help us keep our work tidy.
And the third button uploads files, like pictures, from your computer into your project.
When you choose a file, a pencil and a bin appear next to it. The pencil renames the file, and the bin deletes it.
In the middle is our code editor. This is where we write our instructions for the computer.
And over here, on the right, is our preview. This is where we see what our work looks like.
Up at the top are two important buttons. Save keeps our work safe, and Run shows our latest changes in the preview.

scenes.name: Create index.html
scenes.visual: The cursor clicks the new-file button. A name box appears in the sidebar and 'index.html' types in. Enter: the file appears with its HTML icon and opens in the editor (empty). Then a full-frame explainer: 'HTML = HyperText Markup Language' with the letters building up; a skeleton/frame metaphor drawn as flat boxes.
scenes.camera: Zoom on the sidebar, then cut to the explainer.
scenes.onScreen: index.html · HTML = HyperText Markup Language · STRUCTURE
scenes.sfx: Click, typing, pop when the file appears.

lines.text: Let's create our very first file. Click the new file button.
Type the name index dot html, and press Enter.
lines.caption: Type the name index.html, and press Enter.

lines.text: There it is, in our project area!
HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language.
It is the language that gives a webpage its structure, a bit like the frame that holds up a house.

scenes.name: The Emmet shortcut
scenes.visual: The cursor clicks in the editor. A keyboard overlay (flat keycaps) shows SHIFT held and 1 pressed; '!' appears on line 1 with Emmet's suggestion. The ENTER key presses and the boilerplate expands line by line.
scenes.camera: Push in on the editor. The keyboard overlay sits below the code, above the subtitles.
scenes.sfx: Key clicks, a sparkle on the expansion.

lines.text: Now for a little coding magic. Click inside the code editor.
Hold down the Shift key and press the number one. That types an exclamation mark.
Now press Enter.
Wow! The editor has written a whole webpage starter for us. This shortcut is called Emmet, and it saves us lots of typing.

scenes.name: What each line means
scenes.visual: Large, readable editor (about 34px code). Each line is highlighted as it is named, with a short plain-English label beside it. For <body>, a connector line runs to the preview. For tag pairs, the opening and closing tags light up together with a bracket joining them.
scenes.camera: Code fills the upper area. The subtitle zone stays clear.
scenes.onScreen: Labels: modern HTML · the whole page · language: English · info about the page · letters & symbols · fits any screen · tab name · what we see · opening tag / closing tag

lines.text: Let's look at what each line means.
The doctype line tells the browser that this is a modern HTML document.
lines.caption: The <!DOCTYPE html> line tells the browser that this is a modern HTML document.

lines.text: The html tag is the big container that holds our whole webpage. Lang equals E N tells the browser that our page is in English.
lines.caption: The <html> tag is the big container that holds our whole webpage. lang="en" tells the browser that our page is in English.

lines.text: Inside, we have the head. The head holds information about our page, which we don't see on the page itself.
lines.caption: Inside, we have the <head>. The head holds information about our page, which we don't see on the page itself.

lines.text: The meta charset line helps the browser show letters and symbols correctly.
lines.caption: The meta charset line helps the browser show letters and symbols correctly.

lines.text: The viewport line helps our page fit nicely on phones, tablets and computers.
The title is the name that appears on the browser tab.
And the body holds everything we can actually see on the webpage.
lines.caption: And the <body> holds everything we can actually see on the webpage.

lines.text: Notice how most tags come in pairs: an opening tag, and a closing tag with a forward slash. Everything in between belongs to that element.

scenes.name: Name the page
scenes.visual: The words 'My page' are selected (highlight) and 'Number Match' types in. Inset: a browser tab whose label changes from 'My page' to 'Number Match', among several other tabs.
scenes.camera: Tight on line 6, then pull back to show the tab inset.
scenes.sfx: Typing, pop on the tab change.

lines.text: Let's give our page a proper name.
Select the words My page, and type Number Match.
A meaningful title helps people find our game, even when they have lots of tabs open.

scenes.name: The structure of the game
scenes.visual: Split view: code on the left (only the group being taught is shown, typed at a readable pace, about 26px), a box diagram on the right that builds one nested box per element (main > header, hero, game panel > toolbar, stats, progress, grid, message; footer; win overlay outside main). Each new box flashes when it is named. The closing view shows the whole nesting diagram.
scenes.camera: Code panel scrolls only between groups, never during narration of a line.
scenes.onScreen: Box labels: main.app-shell · header.topbar · section.hero · h1 · section.game-panel · select#difficulty · button#restartButton · .stats (#moves #matched #timer) · .progress-track · #gameGrid · #gameMessage · footer · #winOverlay
scenes.sfx: Typing bursts, a soft thunk as each box lands.

lines.text: Now let's build the structure of our game. We'll go one piece at a time, inside the body.
First, a main element. It holds the main content of our page. We give it a class called app shell, so we can style it later.
lines.caption: First, a <main> element. It holds the main content of our page. We give it a class called app-shell, so we can style it later.

lines.text: Next, the header. It holds our brand: a red N, and the words Number Match.
lines.caption: Next, the <header>. It holds our brand: a red N, and the words Number Match.

lines.text: Then comes the hero section, with a small line of text, a big heading, and a short introduction.
The H 1 tag is our main heading. Every page should have one.
lines.caption: The <h1> tag is our main heading. Every page should have one.

lines.text: Now the game panel. This is where the game itself lives.
At the top is a toolbar. It has a select box, so players can choose Easy, Medium or Challenge, and a Restart button.
Below that, three stat boxes, for the moves, the matched pairs, and the time.
Each number has an I D, like moves or timer. An I D is a unique name, so JavaScript can find it later.
lines.caption: Each number has an id, like moves or timer. An id is a unique name, so JavaScript can find it later.

lines.text: Then a progress track, with a progress fill inside it.
And here is the most important box of all: the game grid. It's empty for now, because JavaScript will create the cards for us.
Under the grid, a message area, to tell the player what is happening.
Then a footer at the bottom of the page.
lines.caption: Then a <footer> at the bottom of the page.

lines.text: Finally, outside the main element, we add the celebration screen. It will appear when every pair is matched.
See how the elements sit inside each other, like boxes inside boxes? That's called nesting.

scenes.name: Save and preview
scenes.visual: Full IDE. The cursor clicks Save (button press plus a check flash), then Run. The preview shows the real unstyled page: default serif text, the heading, a select, a Restart button, MOVES 0 / MATCHED 0 / 6 / TIME 00:00, the message, the footer and the win text. Callout arrows point to the heading, stats and button.
scenes.camera: Zoom from the top bar into the preview.
scenes.sfx: Click + save confirm, click + run whoosh.

lines.text: Time to see our work. Click Save.
Now click Run.
Look at the preview! Our heading, our stats, our buttons and our message are all there.
It looks very plain right now, and that's completely fine. The structure is ready, and that's what matters.

scenes.name: Closing
scenes.visual: The plain page sits centre frame. On o4 a wipe sweeps across it and the plain page turns into the colourful Number Match design (a preview of Lesson 3). End card: 'Next: CSS: Making the Game Beautiful'.
scenes.onScreen: Next: CSS: Making the Game Beautiful
scenes.sfx: Whoosh + sparkle on the transformation, logo sting.
scenes.music: Bed up to full, then out.

lines.text: Fantastic work!
You have created the foundation of your very own game.
But something is missing, isn't it?
Our game needs colour, personality and beautiful cards.
That's exactly what we are going to create in our next lesson with CSS!
